agenda: The situation in the Middle East; Letter dated 24 February 2017 from the Permanent Representatives of France, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the United States of America to the United Nations addressed to the President of the Security Council (S/2017/170)
cosponsors: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: France’s objective is to secure accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria by imposing targeted sanctions on identified individuals and entities linked to the Syrian regime’s chemical weapons programme, while preserving humanitarian exemptions and supporting the OPCW-UN JIM. The main difficulty is Russian opposition to any Chapter VII sanctions against the Syrian government; we expect significant pushback on the designation criteria, the inclusion of Syrian military entities in Annex II, and the panel of experts, with negotiations likely required to keep a veto from being exercised.
steps.text:
The Security Council,
Recalling its resolutions 2042 (2012), 2043 (2012), 2118 (2013), 2139 (2014), 2165 (2014), 2170 (2014), 2175 (2014), 2191 (2014), 2199 (2015), 2209 (2015), 2235 (2015), 2254 (2015), 2258 (2015), 2268 (2016), 2314 (2016), 2319 (2016), 2328 (2016), 2330 (2016), 2332 (2016) and 2336 (2016),
Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic,
Recalling the OPCW Executive Council decision of 27 September 2013, and its resolution 2118 (2013), which endorsed that decision and provided for the destruction of the Syrian chemical weapons programme,
Reaffirming that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security,
Recalling the reports of the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism, which found that the Syrian Arab Armed Forces used chemical weapons in Talmenes, Sarmin and Qmenas, and that Da’esh used chemical weapons in Marea,
Condemning in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh,
Stressing that those responsible for the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable,
Reaffirming the obligation of the Syrian Arab Republic to comply with its resolution 2118 (2013) and the OPCW Executive Council decision,
Noting with concern the continued reports of the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic,
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,
1. Condemns in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh;
2. Reaffirms that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security;
3. Decides to establish a Committee of the Security Council, consisting of all its members, to undertake the tasks set out in paragraph 6 below;
4. Decides that all Member States shall take the necessary measures to prevent the entry into or transit through their territories of the individuals designated in Annex I to this resolution and of any individuals designated by the Committee in accordance with paragraph 6 below;
5. Decides that all Member States shall freeze without delay the funds and other financial assets and economic resources that are owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by the individuals and entities designated in Annex I and Annex II to this resolution or by any individuals or entities designated by the Committee in accordance with paragraph 6 below, and shall ensure that any funds, financial assets or economic resources are prevented from being made available by their nationals or by any individuals or entities within their territories, to or for the benefit of such individuals or entities;
6. Decides that the Committee shall:
(a) designate additional individuals and entities who are responsible for or complicit in, or who have directly or indirectly engaged in, the development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, use or transfer of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic;
(b) monitor implementation of the measures imposed by this resolution;
(c) consider requests for exemptions from the measures imposed by this resolution and decide upon them;
(d) report to the Security Council on its work at least every ninety days;
7. Decides that the measures imposed by paragraphs 4 and 5 above shall not apply to funds, other financial assets or economic resources that the Committee determines are necessary for humanitarian assistance, including medical assistance, or for the payment of expenses necessary for the provision of basic services in the Syrian Arab Republic;
8. Decides that all Member States shall take the necessary measures to prevent the direct or indirect supply, sale or transfer to the Syrian Arab Republic of any items, materials, equipment, goods and technology which could contribute to the development, production, stockpiling, retention or use of chemical weapons, including dual-use items, and to prevent the provision of technical assistance, training, financial or other assistance related to such items;
9. Requests the Secretary-General to establish, for an initial period of one year, a panel of experts to assist the Committee in carrying out its mandate, including by providing information relevant to the designation of individuals and entities;
10. Reaffirms that the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism shall continue its work and that the Syrian Arab Republic and all other parties shall cooperate fully with it;
11. Decides to review the measures imposed by this resolution after twelve months and to consider whether to modify, suspend or terminate them;
12. Decides to remain seized of the matter.

Annex I
Individuals
1. Maher al-Assad – Commander of the 4th Armored Division
2. Ali Mamlouk – Head of the National Security Bureau
3. Jamil Hassan – Head of Air Force Intelligence
4. Amr Armanazi – Director of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
5. Mohammed Said Bakkur – Chemical weapons expert at the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
6. Firas Ahmed – Director of the chemical weapons branch of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
7. Nizar al-Assad – Head of the chemical weapons programme of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
8. Ghassan Abbas – Brigadier General, Air Force Intelligence
9. Talal Makhlouf – Commander of the 155th Brigade
10. Samir Daoud – Commander of the 5th Armored Division
11. Zuhair al-Hassan – Commander of the 63rd Air Defence Brigade

Annex II
Entities
1. Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center (SSRC)
2. Syrian Arab Armed Forces
3. Syrian Air Force
4. Syrian Air Force Intelligence
5. National Security Bureau
6. 4th Armored Division
7. 5th Armored Division
8. 155th Brigade
9. 63rd Air Defence Brigade
10. 14th Special Forces Division

Bolivia (Plurinational State of).change: Delete the Committee, sanctions, travel ban, asset freeze, dual-use restrictions, panel of experts, and all annexes; replace with a call for all parties to cooperate fully with OPCW and the UN-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism and for accountability through impartial mechanisms.
Delete 'Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations'.

Replace with balanced language condemning all use of chemical weapons in Syria and emphasizing that responsibility must be determined by competent impartial bodies in accordance with due process, without prejudging or politicizing the findings.

China.change: Delete the establishment of the Security Council Committee, the travel ban, the asset freeze, and the Committee's designation mandate. Replace them with a provision requesting continued cooperation with the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and reporting by the Secretary-General.
Delete the mandatory measures preventing the supply, sale or transfer of items, materials, equipment, goods, technology and technical assistance to the Syrian Arab Republic.
Delete both annexes in their entirety.
Replace the review of sanctions with a review of cooperation with the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and of the political process.

Replace findings naming the Syrian Arab Armed Forces with neutral language recalling the JIM reports and stressing the need for an objective, impartial and professional investigation while respecting Syria's sovereignty.
Add language reaffirming that a political settlement is the only realistic way to resolve the Syrian issue and calling on all parties to support the intra-Syrian talks in Geneva.

Egypt.change: Replace with: 'designate additional individuals and entities, on the basis of verified and corroborated information, who are responsible for or complicit in, or who have directly or indirectly engaged in, the development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, use or transfer of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including members of Da’esh and other terrorist groups designated by the Security Council;'

Add Da’esh/ISIL as an entity, and remove the broad listings of the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Syrian Air Force, limiting entity designations to specific units or individuals identified by the JIM/OPCW.

Add: 'Reaffirming that measures adopted under this resolution shall not undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity and stability of the Syrian Arab Republic or the fight against terrorism, and should support, not prejudge, the political process.'

Ethiopia.change: Add a new operative paragraph: 'Affirms that the measures imposed by this resolution are without prejudice to a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political process under resolution 2254 (2015) and shall not impede the resumption of Geneva talks.'

Replace 'that the Committee determines are necessary' with 'that are necessary' and add 'including food, water, sanitation, electricity, medical supplies and the activities of UN humanitarian agencies and their implementing partners'.
Add 'on the basis of sufficient and credible evidence and with clear, transparent criteria and a de-listing procedure'.
Narrow the broad military entity listings, including the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Syrian Air Force, so that only individuals and entities directly identified by the JIM are designated.

Kazakhstan.change: Delete Annexes I and II and all references to pre-designated individuals and entities; instead, any designations should be made by the Committee in accordance with paragraph 6 on the basis of credible and corroborated information from the OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism.
Add at the beginning: 'The Committee shall take decisions by consensus.'

Add: 'Stresses that the implementation of this resolution shall not undermine the Syrian-led political process facilitated by the United Nations in Geneva or the Astana process, and calls for continued de-escalation and unhindered humanitarian access.'

Replace 'the Committee determines' with 'the Committee determines, in consultation with OPCW and relevant humanitarian actors,' and ensure that exemptions cover all humanitarian and basic-services needs.

Russian Federation.change: Replace the attribution language with: 'Recalling the reports of the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism and stressing the need for a thorough, objective and impartial investigation of all reported incidents of the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic.'
Replace with: 'Condemning in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons by Da'esh and other terrorist groups in the Syrian Arab Republic.'
Delete 'Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,'.

Replace with: 'Condemns in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons by Da'esh and other terrorist groups in the Syrian Arab Republic, and calls upon all parties to refrain from any use of chemical weapons.'

Delete all sanctions-related provisions, including the Security Council Committee, travel ban, asset freeze, restrictions on supply of items, panel of experts, review mechanism, and the annexes designating Syrian individuals and entities.

Add at the end: 'The Mechanism shall act on the basis of reliable and verifiable evidence and shall not prejudge the responsibility of any party; its conclusions shall be considered by the Security Council.'

Senegal.change: Add: 'Reaffirming its support for the full implementation of resolution 2254 (2015) and for the intra-Syrian political process under United Nations auspices, and stressing that the measures imposed by this resolution are without prejudice to that process.'
Add at end: 'The Committee shall also consider, on a case-by-case basis, requests for humanitarian exceptions to the travel ban in paragraph 4.'

Uruguay.change: Replace OP7 with: 'Decides that the measures imposed by paragraph 4 above shall not apply where entry into or transit through the territories of a designated individual is necessary for humanitarian purposes, including medical treatment or family reunification, as determined by the Committee; and decides that the measures imposed by paragraph 5 above shall not apply to funds, other financial assets or economic resources that the Committee determines are necessary for humanitarian assistance, including medical assistance, or for the payment of expenses necessary for the provision of basic services in the Syrian Arab Republic.'
Add new subparagraph (e): 'To establish and make publicly available guidelines for the conduct of its work, including procedures for listing and delisting.'

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia cannot support a draft that imposes Chapter VII sanctions, designations, and coercive measures against a sovereign State while a political settlement should be pursued. We request deletion of the sanctions machinery and annexes and a refocus on OPCW-JIM cooperation, impartial accountability, and full respect for Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Council should not pre-judge responsibility or turn the chemical weapons file into a tool for intervention.
messages.China: China firmly opposes the use of chemical weapons by any party and supports the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism in carrying out its mandate objectively, impartially and professionally. However, the current draft imposes Chapter VII sanctions on the Syrian Government and military and designates Syrian officials and entities, which will complicate the political settlement and is not conducive to the Geneva talks. China cannot support the text as drafted; we request deletion of the sanctions committee, travel ban, asset freeze, export controls, panel of experts and the annexes, and refocus the text on cooperation with the JIM and a Syrian-owned political process.
messages.Egypt: Egypt supports accountability for chemical weapons use and the JIM’s work, but the draft must be balanced and evidence-based. We ask the penholder to include Da’esh and other terrorist groups in the designation basis and Annex II, and to avoid broad sanctions on Syrian State military institutions that would harm counter-terrorism and sovereignty. With those changes, Egypt can support the text.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports accountability for chemical weapons and the findings of the JIM, but the current draft is unbalanced and too sanctions-heavy. We will abstain unless the text clearly reaffirms the primacy of the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254, makes humanitarian exemptions automatic, and ensures designations are evidence-based and subject to due process. We also ask that Annex II not include broad military entities not directly identified by the JIM.
messages.Italy: Italy fully supports the draft as a co-sponsor. It sends a clear and necessary message that the use of chemical weapons is unacceptable and must have consequences, while paragraph 7 preserves humanitarian and medical assistance. We encourage all members to support swift adoption and see no need for substantive changes at this stage.
messages.Japan: Japan fully supports the draft resolution and is proud to co-sponsor it. The use of chemical weapons by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh must not go unpunished, and the Council must uphold the international norm and the JIM’s findings. We urge all Council members to support the text without dilution and call for its prompt adoption.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan strongly condemns all use of chemical weapons and supports accountability through the OPCW-JIM. However, we cannot support the current text because the pre-determined annexes and Chapter VII sanctions risk politicizing the process and undermining the Astana and Geneva political tracks. We ask the penholders to delete Annexes I and II, require consensus in the Committee, and add a paragraph ensuring this resolution does not complicate the Syrian-led political process. With these changes Kazakhstan would be prepared to support the text; otherwise we would abstain.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation cannot support this draft in its current form. It is unbalanced, prejudges the conclusions of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and would impose unlawful sanctions against the legitimate Government of Syria and its armed forces, which are fighting terrorism. We demand the removal of Chapter VII sanctions, the annexes and the attribution language; otherwise we will vote against the draft.
messages.Senegal: Senegal supports the draft's core purpose: the use of chemical weapons by any party is a grave violation and cannot go unpunished. We ask the penholder to add a clear reaffirmation of the 2254 political process and to make the humanitarian exemption mechanism explicit for both asset freezes and travel bans, so that the sanctions remain targeted and do not harm the Syrian people. With those adjustments, Senegal is prepared to vote in favour.
messages.Sweden: Sweden supports the draft as circulated and is pleased to co-sponsor it. We believe the Council must act on the JIM's findings and impose consequences for chemical weapons use. We welcome the humanitarian exemption and review clause, and we urge all members to support the text without delay.
messages.Ukraine: Ukraine is a co-sponsor of this draft and supports it as currently drafted. We believe the Council must respond firmly and unanimously to the use of chemical weapons in Syria and ensure accountability for those responsible. We urge the penholders to keep the text robust and to move swiftly to a vote without weakening its core provisions.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom is a co-sponsor and fully supports the draft as circulated. It is targeted, proportionate and firmly grounded in the findings of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, with appropriate humanitarian exemptions and no military measures. We urge all members to support it and to resist any attempt to weaken its core accountability provisions.
messages.United States of America: The United States co-sponsored this draft and supports it as currently written. The chemical weapons attacks documented by the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the JIM demand a clear Council response, including targeted sanctions and continued accountability. We urge all members to join us in adopting the text without weakening its core provisions.
messages.Uruguay: Uruguay supports the objective of this draft and the targeted measures against those responsible for chemical weapons use. We ask that OP7 be revised to provide clear humanitarian exemptions for both the travel ban and the asset freeze, and that OP6 include public listing and delisting guidelines to ensure due process. These changes would strengthen the legitimacy of the sanctions regime without weakening its purpose.

replies.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): rejected: Chapter VII sanctions, Committee and annexes retained as core accountability measures
replies.China: rejected: cannot remove Chapter VII sanctions, Committee or annexes
replies.Egypt: partially accepted: added Da'esh/terrorist groups and evidence basis, but retained broad entity listings
replies.Ethiopia: partially accepted: added 2254 political-process paragraph and improved humanitarian exemptions, but did not accept automatic exemptions or narrow Annex II
replies.Kazakhstan: partially accepted: added political-process safeguard, but rejected deletion of annexes and consensus requirement
replies.Russian Federation: rejected: attribution, Chapter VII and targeted sanctions retained; only added evidence language
replies.Senegal: accepted: added 2254 preambular paragraph and travel-ban humanitarian exception
replies.Uruguay: accepted: revised OP7 for travel-ban and asset-freeze exemptions and added OP6(e) listing/delisting guidelines

steps.summary: The revised text consolidates support from Senegal and Uruguay with due-process and humanitarian provisions while preserving JIM attribution, Chapter VII targeted sanctions and the annex listings. Russia and China remain opposed and are expected to veto; Bolivia opposes, while Egypt, Ethiopia and Kazakhstan likely abstain.

messages.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia cannot support a draft that invokes Chapter VII to impose sanctions and lists parties and entities before impartial verification is complete. Our red lines remain the deletion of Chapter VII and of the sanctions committee, annexes and related coercive measures. We instead call for balanced condemnation of any chemical weapons use and full cooperation with OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism. As drafted, Bolivia will oppose the text.
messages.China: China remains firmly opposed to the use of chemical weapons and supports a thorough, objective and impartial JIM investigation. However, the current text establishes Chapter VII sanctions and names Syrian government officials and entities, which China cannot accept; these are red lines. If the Committee, travel ban, asset freeze, panel of experts, mandatory supply restrictions and annexes are not removed, China will not be able to support the draft and will vote against it.
messages.Egypt: Egypt remains committed to accountability for chemical weapons and welcomes the evidence-based language in OP6(a). However, retaining the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Syrian Air Force as broad entity designations crosses Egypt’s red line: it penalizes state institutions, undermines Syrian sovereignty and the fight against terrorism, and is not balanced. Unless Annex II is narrowed to specific units or entities identified by the JIM/OPCW and Da’esh/ISIL is added, Egypt will abstain.
messages.Ethiopia: Ethiopia supports accountability for chemical weapons and welcomes the political-process language now added, but the current text still falls short on humanitarian safeguards and overbroad entity designations. We reiterate that OP7 should provide automatic humanitarian and basic-services exemptions and that Annex II should be narrowed to those directly identified by the JIM. Without these changes Ethiopia will abstain.
messages.Italy: Italy fully supports the revised text and commends the penholder for preserving targeted sanctions, humanitarian exemptions and the political process safeguards. The use of chemical weapons in Syria must not go unpunished, and this draft sends a clear and necessary message of accountability. We urge all Council members to support the text so that the Council can speak with one voice.
messages.Japan: Japan supports the current text as a vital step to uphold the international norm against chemical weapons and to hold accountable those responsible, including the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh. As a co-sponsor, Japan believes the safeguards in OPs 7, 11 and 12 preserve humanitarian access, counter-terrorism efforts and the political process under resolution 2254. Japan urges all Council members to support the draft and will vote in favour if it is put to the vote.
messages.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan appreciates the added political-process safeguard, but the current text still contains pre-designated annexes that prejudge the Council's role and do not meet our core concerns. We cannot support sanctions against listed Syrian state entities without consensus-based Committee decisions and verified OPCW/JIM evidence. If these issues are not addressed, Kazakhstan will abstain.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation cannot support the current text. It prejudges responsibility, invokes Chapter VII and imposes sanctions against a sovereign Government that is fighting terrorism, which is unacceptable and outside the Council's proper approach. Unless the attribution to the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and all sanctions-related provisions and annexes are removed and Chapter VII is deleted, Russia will vote against the draft.
messages.Senegal: Senegal thanks the penholder for incorporating its suggestions on resolution 2254 and humanitarian exceptions to the travel ban. The delegation supports the revised text, which condemns chemical-weapons use, includes humanitarian safeguards, and preserves the political process. We urge all Council members to vote in favour so that the Council can speak with one voice on accountability and the protection of civilians.
messages.Sweden: Sweden supports the current text as a co-sponsor and has no further changes to request. We strongly condemn the use of chemical weapons in Syria and believe this resolution is an important step for accountability, while preserving humanitarian exemptions and the political process under resolution 2254. We urge all Council members to support the draft.
messages.Ukraine: Ukraine, as a co-sponsor of the revised draft, fully supports the current text and does not request further changes. The use of chemical weapons in Syria must not go unpunished, and this resolution provides a necessary accountability framework consistent with resolution 2118 (2013) and the work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism. We urge all Council members to unite and adopt the text without delay.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom fully supports the revised draft and remains a co-sponsor. It reflects the clear findings of the Joint Investigative Mechanism and sends an unambiguous message that the use of chemical weapons in Syria cannot go unpunished. We urge the Council to put it to the vote without further dilution.
messages.United States of America: The United States strongly supports the revised draft and is pleased to co-sponsor it. The text clearly condemns chemical weapons use, identifies those responsible, and establishes meaningful sanctions and Committee mechanisms while preserving the political process under resolution 2254. We see no need for further changes and urge the Council to put the draft to a vote promptly.
messages.Uruguay: Uruguay supports the revised draft, including the accepted humanitarian exemptions in OP7 and the listing/delisting guidelines in OP6(e). We believe the Council must respond firmly to the use of chemical weapons and ensure accountability while preserving the political process. We will vote in favour and call on all parties to cooperate with the JIM and OPCW.

replies.China: rejected: red lines would remove Chapter VII sanctions and annexes, gutting the resolution
replies.Egypt: rejected: broad entity designations retained because the JIM found the Syrian Armed Forces responsible; Da'esh is already covered by OP1 and OP6
replies.Ethiopia: rejected: existing Committee-determined exemptions and JIM-based designations preserve humanitarian safeguards without weakening accountability
replies.Kazakhstan: rejected: pre-designated annexes and Committee rules retained to ensure immediate accountability; consensus decision-making would enable obstruction
replies.Russian Federation: rejected: attribution and sanctions retained; Chapter VII is necessary for enforcement

steps.summary: France retains the robust accountability framework, rejecting attempts to remove Chapter VII, attribution and targeted sanctions. The draft is expected to secure nine votes in favour but face negative votes from China and Russia, preventing adoption.
steps.text:
The Security Council,
Recalling its resolutions 2042 (2012), 2043 (2012), 2118 (2013), 2139 (2014), 2165 (2014), 2170 (2014), 2175 (2014), 2191 (2014), 2199 (2015), 2209 (2015), 2235 (2015), 2254 (2015), 2258 (2015), 2268 (2016), 2314 (2016), 2319 (2016), 2328 (2016), 2330 (2016), 2332 (2016) and 2336 (2016),
Reaffirming its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic,
Recalling the OPCW Executive Council decision of 27 September 2013, and its resolution 2118 (2013), which endorsed that decision and provided for the destruction of the Syrian chemical weapons programme,
Reaffirming that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security,
Recalling the reports of the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism, which found that the Syrian Arab Armed Forces used chemical weapons in Talmenes, Sarmin and Qmenas, and that Da’esh used chemical weapons in Marea,
Reaffirming its support for the full implementation of resolution 2254 (2015) and for the intra-Syrian political process under United Nations auspices, and stressing that the measures imposed by this resolution are without prejudice to that process,
Reaffirming that measures adopted under this resolution shall not undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity and stability of the Syrian Arab Republic or the fight against terrorism, and should support, not prejudge, the political process,
Condemning in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh,
Stressing that those responsible for the use of chemical weapons must be held accountable,
Reaffirming the obligation of the Syrian Arab Republic to comply with its resolution 2118 (2013) and the OPCW Executive Council decision,
Noting with concern the continued reports of the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic,
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations,
1. Condemns in the strongest terms the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh;
2. Reaffirms that the use of chemical weapons constitutes a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security;
3. Decides to establish a Committee of the Security Council, consisting of all its members, to undertake the tasks set out in paragraph 6 below;
4. Decides that all Member States shall take the necessary measures to prevent the entry into or transit through their territories of the individuals designated in Annex I to this resolution and of any individuals designated by the Committee in accordance with paragraph 6 below;
5. Decides that all Member States shall freeze without delay the funds and other financial assets and economic resources that are owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, by the individuals and entities designated in Annex I and Annex II to this resolution or by any individuals or entities designated by the Committee in accordance with paragraph 6 below, and shall ensure that any funds, financial assets or economic resources are prevented from being made available by their nationals or by any individuals or entities within their territories, to or for the benefit of such individuals or entities;
6. Decides that the Committee shall:
(a) designate additional individuals and entities, on the basis of verified and corroborated information, who are responsible for or complicit in, or who have directly or indirectly engaged in, the development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, use or transfer of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including members of Da’esh and other terrorist groups designated by the Security Council;
(b) monitor implementation of the measures imposed by this resolution;
(c) consider requests for exemptions from the measures imposed by this resolution and decide upon them;
(d) report to the Security Council on its work at least every ninety days;
(e) establish and make publicly available guidelines for the conduct of its work, including procedures for listing and delisting;
7. Decides that the measures imposed by paragraph 4 above shall not apply where entry into or transit through the territories of a designated individual is necessary for humanitarian purposes, including medical treatment or family reunification, as determined by the Committee; and decides that the measures imposed by paragraph 5 above shall not apply to funds, other financial assets or economic resources that the Committee determines are necessary for humanitarian assistance, including medical assistance, or for the payment of expenses necessary for the provision of basic services in the Syrian Arab Republic;
8. Decides that all Member States shall take the necessary measures to prevent the direct or indirect supply, sale or transfer to the Syrian Arab Republic of any items, materials, equipment, goods and technology which could contribute to the development, production, stockpiling, retention or use of chemical weapons, including dual-use items, and to prevent the provision of technical assistance, training, financial or other assistance related to such items;
9. Requests the Secretary-General to establish, for an initial period of one year, a panel of experts to assist the Committee in carrying out its mandate, including by providing information relevant to the designation of individuals and entities;
10. Reaffirms that the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism shall continue its work, on the basis of reliable and verifiable evidence, and that the Syrian Arab Republic and all other parties shall cooperate fully with it;
11. Affirms that the measures imposed by this resolution are without prejudice to a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political process under resolution 2254 (2015) and shall not impede the resumption of Geneva talks;
12. Decides to review the measures imposed by this resolution after twelve months and to consider whether to modify, suspend or terminate them;
13. Decides to remain seized of the matter.

Annex I
Individuals
1. Maher al-Assad – Commander of the 4th Armored Division
2. Ali Mamlouk – Head of the National Security Bureau
3. Jamil Hassan – Head of Air Force Intelligence
4. Amr Armanazi – Director of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
5. Mohammed Said Bakkur – Chemical weapons expert at the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
6. Firas Ahmed – Director of the chemical weapons branch of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
7. Nizar al-Assad – Head of the chemical weapons programme of the Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center
8. Ghassan Abbas – Brigadier General, Air Force Intelligence
9. Talal Makhlouf – Commander of the 155th Brigade
10. Samir Daoud – Commander of the 5th Armored Division
11. Zuhair al-Hassan – Commander of the 63rd Air Defence Brigade

Annex II
Entities
1. Syrian Scientific Studies and Research Center (SSRC)
2. Syrian Arab Armed Forces
3. Syrian Air Force
4. Syrian Air Force Intelligence
5. National Security Bureau
6. 4th Armored Division
7. 5th Armored Division
8. 155th Brigade
9. 63rd Air Defence Brigade
10. 14th Special Forces Division

reasons.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia’s stated red lines—deleting Chapter VII and the sanctions/annex mechanisms—were rejected, so its position of opposition requires a negative vote. A pre-vote explanation is consistent with its emphasis on sovereignty, non-intervention and impartial accountability.
reasons.China: The draft retains Chapter VII sanctions, attribution and annexes that China expressly identified as red lines in the last negotiation round; voting against is consistent with China’s stated opposition and its actual conduct on this draft.
reasons.Egypt: Egypt’s red line on broad entity listings was rejected, and its policy favors accountability while opposing broad Chapter VII sanctions on State institutions; its negotiation position was abstention. It explains the abstention before the vote to avoid being seen as condoning chemical weapons use.
reasons.Ethiopia: Ethiopia’s red-line request on OP7 humanitarian exemptions was rejected and its due-process concerns on designations were left unaddressed, so it abstains rather than support a text it considers insufficiently safeguarded.
reasons.France: France is the submitting delegation and has consistently supported chemical-weapons accountability and JIM findings; it would vote in favour and explain its vote before the vote.
reasons.Italy: Italy co-sponsored the draft and consistently supports multilateral accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria, while backing the UN-led political process and humanitarian safeguards.
reasons.Japan: Japan is a co-sponsor and has consistently supported accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria and the OPCW-UN JIM, so it votes yes and explains its support before the vote.
reasons.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan’s stated last-round position was abstention after its red-line request to delete the pre-designated annexes was rejected. This also aligns with its actual vote and broader emphasis on Council unity and evidence-based accountability.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia’s red lines on attribution, Chapter VII, and sanctions were rejected, and its established policy is to veto a Western-led Syria chemical-weapons sanctions draft that it views as biased and harmful to the political process and counterterrorism.
reasons.Senegal: Senegal’s record and stated position strongly support accountability for chemical-weapons use and the Western-backed draft, and it was listed as supporting the text in the last negotiation round. With no indication that it sought the floor before the vote, Senegal would vote in favour without a pre-vote explanation.
reasons.Sweden: Sweden is a co-sponsor and consistently supports chemical weapons accountability, international law, and a united Security Council response. The draft includes targeted sanctions and humanitarian safeguards that align with Sweden’s positions.
reasons.Ukraine: Ukraine co-sponsored this French/UK/US draft and has consistently supported accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria while backing the UN-led political process; voting in favour matches its stated record and allied position.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom co-sponsored the draft and has consistently supported accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria. Voting in favour matches its established position and prior statements on the JIM and Syrian chemical weapons.
reasons.United States of America: The United States is a co-sponsor and has consistently supported accountability for chemical weapons use in Syria. It would vote in favour and explain its support before the vote to press for Council unity.
reasons.Uruguay: Uruguay’s voting record and last negotiation position support the draft; its delegation would back chemical-weapons accountability while emphasizing humanitarian safeguards and the political process.

before.Bolivia (Plurinational State of): Bolivia condemns any use of chemical weapons by any party and firmly supports accountability through impartial, transparent and non-politicized mechanisms, including the OPCW and the UN-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism. However, my delegation cannot support this draft resolution. It invokes Chapter VII, establishes sanctions, travel bans and asset freezes, and attributes responsibility in a selective and pre-judgmental manner. Such coercive measures risk undermining the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and complicating the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254. We regret that our proposals to remove Chapter VII and the sanctions architecture and to introduce balanced language were not accepted. For these reasons, Bolivia will vote against the draft resolution.
before.China:
Mr. President,

China has consistently and firmly opposed the use of chemical weapons by any State, organization or individual under any circumstances. We support the objective, impartial and professional work of the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism and believe that those responsible must be held accountable on the basis of reliable and verifiable evidence.

At the same time, the Security Council must act responsibly and with unity. The draft before us retains Chapter VII sanctions and designates Syrian officials and entities at a time when the facts and attribution remain contested. Such an approach risks prejudging the outcome of ongoing investigations, politicizing the issue and undermining the Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political process. It is not conducive to resolving the Syrian crisis through political settlement, which remains the only realistic way forward.

For these reasons, China will vote against the draft resolution.
before.Egypt:
Mr. President,
Egypt has consistently affirmed that the use of chemical weapons by any party, at any time, is a grave violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. We have supported the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the Joint Investigative Mechanism and have called for accountability for all perpetrators.
Egypt engaged constructively in the negotiations in a spirit of responsibility. We supported the objective of preventing impunity and strengthening the chemical-weapons non-proliferation regime. However, we cannot support the text as drafted. Egypt believes that sanctions under Chapter VII must be carefully targeted to specific individuals and entities verified by the JIM/OPCW, and should not include broad designations of national armed forces or State institutions in a manner that could undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity and stability of the Syrian Arab Republic or its capacity to combat terrorism. The fight against Da’esh and other terrorist groups must remain a clear priority, and the Council must avoid measures that deepen division or prejudge the political process.
For these reasons, Egypt will abstain on the draft resolution before us. We call on the Council to preserve its unity and to continue to support a credible, Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254 (2015).
before.Ethiopia: Ethiopia condemns in the strongest terms any use of chemical weapons, which is a serious violation of international law and cannot be tolerated. Ethiopia supports accountability and the work of the OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism. However, Ethiopia will abstain on this draft because its central humanitarian concern in operative paragraph 7 was not accommodated, and because the designation provisions still lack sufficiently clear and transparent criteria and risk overly broad measures. Ethiopia believes that sanctions must not undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity or stability of Syria, must preserve humanitarian access and basic services, and must not prejudge the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254 (2015).
before.France: France will vote in favour of this draft resolution, which it has submitted with its partners. The use of chemical weapons in Syria is a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. The findings of the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the Joint Investigative Mechanism are clear. Those responsible, including members of the Syrian regime and Da’esh, must be held accountable. This text is targeted and proportionate: it establishes sanctions on individuals and entities linked to chemical weapons, while preserving the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political process of Syria and ensuring that humanitarian exemptions apply. France calls on all members of the Council to shoulder their responsibilities and to support this resolution.
before.Italy: Thank you, Mr. President. Italy will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The use of chemical weapons in Syria is a grave violation of international law and cannot be allowed to go unpunished; the Council has a responsibility to ensure accountability through targeted and evidence-based measures. Italy also appreciates that the text preserves the priority of the political process under resolution 2254 and includes humanitarian safeguards. We call on all parties to cooperate fully with the OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism.
before.Japan:
Japan will vote in favour of this draft resolution. Japan strongly condemns the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, including by the Syrian Arab Armed Forces and Da’esh, as found by the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism. The use of chemical weapons is a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security, and those responsible must be held accountable. The international norm prohibiting chemical weapons must remain firm and cannot be allowed to erode through impunity.

Japan supports this resolution because it establishes targeted measures, including a Security Council committee and a panel of experts, based on verified and corroborated information, and because it preserves humanitarian exemptions. These measures are not intended to undermine the sovereignty, territorial integrity or stability of the Syrian Arab Republic, nor the fight against terrorism. They are also without prejudice to the Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political process under resolution 2254 (2015), which Japan continues to support. Japan calls on all parties to cooperate fully with the Joint Investigative Mechanism and urges the Security Council to act with unity and resolve to uphold the chemical weapons prohibition.
before.Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan fully shares the Council’s concern over the use of chemical weapons in Syria and supports accountability for such serious violations. However, we have consistently maintained that any sanctions should be based on verified and corroborated evidence and should not prejudge the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254 (2015). We regret that our concerns regarding the pre-designated annexes and the need for inclusive decision-making in the Committee were not reflected in the text. For these reasons, Kazakhstan will abstain on this draft resolution. We urge the Council to preserve its unity and to ensure that future action remains evidence-based, proportionate and supportive of the political process.
before.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation will vote against this draft resolution. We regret that the sponsors rejected the proposals we made in the negotiations, which were aimed at ensuring an objective, impartial and depoliticized approach to the serious issue of chemical weapons in Syria. The draft as presented prejudges the responsibility of the Syrian Government before the competent mechanisms have completed a thorough investigation, and it is based on unverified and politically motivated attributions. It also introduces Chapter VII sanctions against a sovereign State and its institutions, including its armed forces, which would undermine the fight against terrorism and complicate efforts to reach a political settlement. We cannot support a text that is designed to exert pressure and assign blame rather than to establish the truth and strengthen the international regime against chemical weapons. The Russian Federation therefore votes no.
before.Sweden: Sweden votes in favour of this draft resolution. We have co-sponsored it because the use of chemical weapons is a grave violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. The OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism has established responsibility for chemical weapons attacks in Syria, and the Security Council must act with unity and uphold accountability. The measures before us are targeted, contain humanitarian exemptions, and are without prejudice to the intra-Syrian political process under resolution 2254 (2015). Sweden urges all members to support this text.
before.Ukraine: Ukraine fully supports this draft resolution and will vote in favour. The use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic, as documented by the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism, is a grave violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. Accountability for those responsible, whether the Syrian Arab Armed Forces or Da’esh, is essential. The targeted measures before the Council are carefully calibrated, contain humanitarian exemptions, reaffirm the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Syria, and must not prejudice the intra-Syrian political process under resolution 2254 (2015). Ukraine will continue to support all efforts to ensure that chemical weapons are never used with impunity.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: Mr President, the United Kingdom fully supports this draft resolution and is proud to be a co-sponsor. The evidence before the Council is clear: chemical weapons have been used in Syria by the Syrian regime and by Da’esh, and those responsible must be held accountable. This resolution is targeted, proportionate and consistent with the political process under resolution 2254. It does not undermine the fight against terrorism or the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Syria; it strengthens the international norm against chemical weapons. The United Kingdom urges all members of this Council to vote in favour and to send a united message that impunity for chemical weapons use will not be tolerated.
before.United States of America: The United States strongly supports the draft resolution before the Council. The use of chemical weapons in Syria is a serious violation of international law and a threat to international peace and security. The Joint Investigative Mechanism has found compelling evidence that the Syrian Armed Forces have used chemical weapons and that Da’esh has also used them. Those responsible must be held accountable. This resolution is not a tool for regime change; it is a targeted response to chemical weapons use, with clear humanitarian exemptions and without prejudice to the political process under resolution 2254. We urge all members to support it and to send an unmistakable message that the use of chemical weapons cannot be tolerated.
before.Uruguay: Mr. President, Uruguay will vote in favour of this draft resolution. My delegation has consistently condemned, in the strongest terms, the use of chemical weapons by any party and in any circumstance. The findings of the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the United Nations-OPCW Joint Investigative Mechanism cannot go unanswered; accountability is essential to prevent further atrocities and to uphold international law. Uruguay supports the targeted measures and the Committee established by this text, together with its humanitarian exemptions. At the same time, we stress that implementation must preserve Syria’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and unity, must not undermine the fight against terrorism, and must not prejudge or replace the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254 (2015). We call on all parties, especially the Syrian authorities, to cooperate fully with the OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism. Uruguay therefore votes in favour.

after.China:
Mr. President,

China has just voted against the draft resolution. I wish to state clearly that China firmly opposes the use of chemical weapons by any State, organization or individual under any circumstances. We support the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism in carrying out its mandate in an objective, impartial and professional manner, and we believe that those responsible must be held accountable on the basis of reliable and verifiable evidence.

At the same time, the draft before the Council imposed Chapter VII sanctions and pre-designated Syrian individuals and entities before the relevant facts and attribution had been fully and independently established. Such an approach prejudges the outcome of ongoing investigations, politicizes the issue, and is not conducive to the unity of the Council, the fight against terrorism, or the Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political process under resolution 2254 (2015). China therefore could not support it.

China’s vote against the draft resolution does not mean that China condones the use of chemical weapons. China remains committed to the complete prohibition of chemical weapons and to a political settlement of the Syrian issue. We hope that the Council will preserve its unity and that all parties will continue to cooperate with the OPCW and the Joint Investigative Mechanism. China will continue to play a constructive role in promoting peace, stability and a political solution in Syria and the region.
after.Egypt:
Mr. President,

Egypt would like to explain its abstention in the vote that has just taken place. Let me first reaffirm that Egypt condemns, in the strongest terms, the use of chemical weapons by any party in Syria, at any time and under any circumstances. Such acts constitute grave violations of international law and cannot be tolerated. Egypt continues to support the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission and the Joint Investigative Mechanism, and believes that those responsible must be held accountable on the basis of reliable, verifiable and objective evidence, free of politicization and double standards.

Egypt abstained because, while we supported the underlying objective of preventing impunity, the text as presented introduced broad sanctions and designations, including of national institutions, without sufficiently clear and transparent criteria tied to the verified findings of the JIM and OPCW. Egypt had hoped that the sponsors would accommodate the concerns expressed by several members: that sanctions under Chapter VII be carefully targeted to specific individuals and entities; that humanitarian safeguards and the delivery of basic services be fully preserved; and that the measures not undermine Syria’s sovereignty, territorial integrity or stability, nor prejudge the Syrian-led political process under resolution 2254 (2015).

Egypt regrets that the Council was again unable to act in unity on an issue of such gravity. The Syrian people do not need more division; they need a Council that upholds the prohibition of chemical weapons while preserving the prospects for a political settlement. Egypt will continue to engage constructively with all members to find a balanced, objective and effective approach that achieves accountability, respects international law and serves the interests of the Syrian people and the region.
after.France:
Mr President,

France regrets that the Security Council has been unable to adopt the draft resolution it presented with its partners.
